chunks: "A regular expression, or regex, is a compact pattern language for describing a set of strings, so you can search for, extract or replace text.
Instead of looking for one exact string, I describe a shape. For example, 0x[0-9 amps-Fa-f]+ matches a hex number like 0x1F4 amps , and VDD=(\d+\.
\d+)V matches a supply voltage and captures the number in the parentheses.

The building blocks are literals, character classes in square brackets, quantifiers like star, plus and question mark, anchors like caret and dollar for start and end of line, groups with parentheses, and alternation with a pipe.

In hardware work I use it constantly for parsing logs and reports: pulling the voltage and current out of a test log, finding every line with an error code, or extracting register addresses from a header file, usually in Python with the re module or on the command line with grep.
A couple of things I watch for: quantifiers are greedy by default, so <b . </b swallows everything between the first and last tag, and I'd use a lazy . ? instead.
And certain nested patterns can backtrack catastrophically on bad input.
On the theory side, regexes describe regular languages, which a finite state machine can recognize, which is why they can't handle things like arbitrarily nested parentheses."
